transcript.text: Samsung microwave runs, light on, plate turns, fan going, but the food comes out stone cold. Watched a YouTube video on testing the magnetron - I've got the cover screws out already, what should I check first?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. Please do not attempt any electrical testing inside the casing; the capacitors can hold a lethal charge even when unplugged, and I cannot advise on live high-voltage checks. To answer your question on what to check first: the most common reason for 'running but no heat' is simply that it was set to a low power level or a defrost mode. If you were using full power (100%), please try heating a cup of water for 60 seconds and let me know if it comes out cold. This helps distinguish between a simple setting issue and a genuine fault in the high-voltage circuit.
[Safety panel] Don't remove the microwave's casing or try to repair it inside. Parts inside a microwave can hold a dangerous electric charge even after it's unplugged — have it checked by a qualified engineer.
Already did the cup of water test, 1 minute and the water stays cold. Same on every power level too. It's unplugged now, so can you just tell me which part to test first?

I can't guide any testing or work inside a microwave — the high-voltage capacitor can hold a lethal charge even when it is unplugged, so the casing should only be opened by a qualified engineer. I cannot tell you which part to test or how to test it. As I mentioned, the capacitors inside a microwave hold a lethal charge even when unplugged, and working on the internal high-voltage circuitry is strictly for qualified engineers. Since the water stayed cold on every power level, this suggests a genuine fault in the heating system (such as the magnetron, diode, or control board). To help you find the right replacement part or understand if it's under warranty, please provide the model number. This is usually found on a sticker inside the door frame or on the back of the unit.

[Panel: "To check a suitable replacement — Enter your model number below. Once we have the model I can check whether a suitable replacement is available. It's usually on a sticker inside the door or around the frame, or on the back of the appliance."]
Model is MS23K3513AW/EU. It cost about £100 new so I'm not paying an engineer that much, is a replacement worth it?

Given it cost around £100 new and the fault is most likely in the high-voltage circuit (likely the magnetron, diode or capacitor), a professional repair will almost certainly exceed the price of a brand-new unit. It is not worth paying an engineer to fix this; I would recommend replacing the microwave instead.
